A1:
**A1: Calls isAvailable with a String argument (1 point)**

Award the point as soon as the response contains at least one syntactically correct invocation of the availability method with a String argument. Read the call generously: an unqualified call such as `isAvailable(requestedName)` written inside the `Account` class counts as calling on the class/`this` implicitly (use of `this` is optional), and a call on a reference whose type is `Account` — e.g. `acct.isAvailable(s)` or `new Account(...).isAvailable(s)` — also counts, since the receiver is still an Account and the call compiles. The argument need only be evidently intended as the candidate username string: an undeclared `name` variable, a value the student treats as text, or a call written with the type word included all pass, since passing a String other than the parameter is explicitly tolerated. Minor spelling or capitalization variants of the method name (`isAvailible`, `IsAvailable`, `is_available`) are not deducted so long as context makes the intended call to the availability method unambiguous; the point is for making the call, not for spelling it. If the response makes one correct call plus some other stray or leftover invocation elsewhere that is malformed, still award the point — one good call anywhere suffices.

Deduct only when there is no correct call anywhere: i.e., every invocation uses an explicit receiver that is not `Account` or `this` (for example a `String`, a `Scanner`, or a student-invented unrelated class/object), or the only argument passed is clearly not intended as a username string (such as a bare loop counter used as a number), or no call to the availability method is made at all.
A2:
**A2 — Updates potential usernames until an available username is found**

Award the point only if the response actually tests availability by calling the availability-check method (`isAvailable`) on a potential username and, within the body of the loop, updates the potential username before testing again. The call may be made incorrectly, `requestedName` may go unused, and the update of the potential username may itself be wrong — none of that costs the point, because the credit here is for the structure of repeatedly checking availability and revising the candidate name.

Deduct if no availability test exists at all: in particular, if the constructor never calls `isAvailable` anywhere and simply assigns the requested name directly to `username`, there is no availability logic, so the point is not earned. Also deduct if the response checks availability but does so without a potential username, or if it loops without updating a potential username inside the loop body.
A3:
**A3 (Increments a count in the context of a loop) — grading note**

Award the point (no_deduct) whenever the response advances a counter once per repeated attempt at finding an available username, regardless of the syntax used to repeat. A `for`/`while`/`do-while` loop containing a statement such as `count++`, `count += 1`, or `count = count + 1` qualifies, and so does any equivalent repeated-attempt structure, including a recursive helper method invoked with `count + 1` — the intent of this item is that the counter advances per attempt, not that a particular loop construct appear. Do not require the counter to be used in building a candidate username, and do not require it to be initialized; consistent with the explicit allowance for "fail to initialize the count," a counter variable that is never declared anywhere (so that the code would not compile) still earns the point as long as the increment statement appears inside the loop or per-attempt recursive call.

Deduct only if no counter is advanced per repetition attempt at all — i.e., there is no increment (or `count + 1` style advance) tied to the repeated attempts, or the increment occurs outside any repetition mechanism so that it cannot advance once per attempt.
